Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.
Machine Learning.comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Code at https://github.com/a1bhinav/puzzling-bench and data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/puzzling-bench/puzzling-bench

Machine Learning.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
Machine Learning.summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 19 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables. Code: https://github.com/PriorLabs/matsci-bo-bench

Machine Learning.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
Machine Learning.summary: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

Machine Learning.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective
Machine Learning.summary: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.

Machine Learning.title: Interpretable identification of constitutive parameter field for three-dimensional heterogeneous and graded hyperelastic materials from full-field displacements
Machine Learning.summary: The inverse problem of identifying spatially varying material properties of heterogeneous solids using experimentally available displacement fields and boundary reaction forces alone remains challenging. Being able to characterize heterogeneous and graded solids would be advantageous in the design and manufacturing of functionally graded materials and composites. Additionally, an efficient technique for identifying heterogeneous material properties from in vivo measurements would be useful in biomedical contexts to characterize heterogeneous biological tissues. Although several techniques developed over the past two decades have addressed inverse identification for homogeneous materials, including linear elastic, hyperelastic, viscoelastic, and elastoplastic solids, comparatively fewer studies have considered heterogeneous and graded materials. Furthermore, several recent approaches to characterizing heterogeneous and graded materials employ parameter-heavy, deep learning-based frameworks trained to enforce force equilibrium at specified collocation points within the material. In this work, we propose an interpretable and time-efficient framework that predicts the three-dimensional relative spatial variation of a constitutive parameter field for multiple parameters of a heterogeneous hyperelastic material, using only displacement-field data. In this work, we validate our framework on 3D synthetic and 2D experimental benchmarks involving heterogeneous, graded, and anisotropic hyperelastic materials. By leveraging the linear nature of the inverse problem for hyperelastic materials and directly optimizing for the constitutive parameters at the finite-element level, we achieve acceptable prediction accuracy with significantly lower computational time compared to recently reported deep-learning-based frameworks.

Machine Learning.title: Protecting Confidentiality, Privacy and Integrity in Collaborative Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
A collaboration between dataset owners and model owners is needed for effective machine learning (ML) training. During this collaboration, however, dataset owners and model owners want to protect the confidentiality of their respective assets (i.e., datasets, models and training code), with the dataset owners also caring about the privacy of individual users whose data is in the datasets. Existing solutions provide limited confidentiality for models and training code, suffer from data privacy issues, or incur unacceptable performance.
  We present Citadel++, a collaborative ML training system to simultaneously protect the confidentiality of datasets, models and training code as well as the privacy of individual user data. Specifically, Citadel++ takes a chained approach. First, we employ the Virtual Machine-level Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) as the training runtime to provide confidentiality protections for datasets, model and training code. Second, we create a privacy barrier that improves upon differential privacy techniques to safeguard the privacy of individual user data while maintaining model utility. Third, we construct and optimize a Virtual Machine Privilege Level (VMPL)-enforced fine-grained sandbox to regulate the dataflow in the system to ensure that our privacy barrier is always applied even when the model and training code maybe maliciously designed. Finally, we employ specific TEE capabilities to ensure the integrity of our privacy barrier and sandboxing mechanisms for their correct execution.
  To our knowledge, Citadel++ is the first collaborative training system providing strong confidentiality and privacy protections for dataset owners and model owners simultaneously. We analyze Citadel++ security properties and implement a full prototype. Our evaluation shows that Citadel++ provides strong guarantees with modest overheads.

Machine Learning.title: RAP: Radial-Angular Random Projection for Hyperbolic Representations
Machine Learning.summary: Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.

Optimization and Control.title: Adaptive Control Barrier Functions for Nonlinear Singularly Perturbed Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have emerged as a flexible and efficient approach for enforcing dynamic safety constraints. In this paper, we consider a class of uncertain nonlinear systems with singular perturbations and develop an adaptive CBF framework for such systems to enforce safety constraints on both the slow and fast subsystems in the overall singularly perturbed nonlinear system with uncertain parameters. We first develop a robustness property showing that if an adaptive controller for the slow subsystem satisfies the slow CBF condition with an appropriate safety margin, then for sufficiently small values of the singular perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$, the slow subsystem remains within an $O(\varepsilon)$-neighborhood of its safe set. We then consider the more general case of safety constraints on both the fast and slow subsystems and provide conditions under which joint slow-fast safety is achieved despite the parametric uncertainties. The reduced-order slow model and the slow and fast CBF conditions are evaluated using an online parameter estimate and the parameter mismatch between the estimated and true reduced-order models is addressed via a state-dependent robustness margin in the CBF inequalities. To illustrate the proposed framework, we present simulation studies for two systems with parametric uncertainties: a synthetic two-time-scale fourth-order example system and a unicycle with a fast turn-rate actuator and an obstacle avoidance safety constraint.

Optimization and Control.title: Time-optimal travel driven by two vector fields on a Riemannian manifold
Optimization and Control.summary: We study minimum-time travel on a Riemannian manifold $(M,h)$ for a kinematic model in which finitely many drift fields contribute additively to the velocity, after independent rescaling of their components parallel and orthogonal to a chosen unit direction $u$. The velocity is then $\mathcal Y_x(u)=(η(x)+h_x(\widehat Z_x,u))u+\widehat W_x$, $u\in UT_xM$, for two effective vector fields $\widehat Z$, $\widehat W$ and a self-propulsion speed $η\geq0$. Let $F$ be the gauge of the radial hull $\mathcal B_x=[0,1]\cdot\mathcal S_x$ of the velocity set $\mathcal S_x=\mathcal Y_x(UT_xM)$. Where $η>0$, we characterize when $F$ is a Finsler metric and give two-sided estimates and representation formulae for it; where $η=0$ and $\widehat Z\neq0$, we recover the Randers, Kropina and strong-wind regimes of Zermelo navigation. Examples include Matsumoto's slope metric, traction-modified slope models, and alternative models for wildfire propagation and microswimmer navigation. Since $F$ need not be a Finsler metric, we treat the minimum-time problem with tools from differential inclusions. For distinct endpoints, the inclusions defined by $\mathcal S_x$ and $\mathcal B_x$ give the same infimum travel time, and so does the convex hull of $\mathcal B_x$ under local controllability at the terminal point. When $F$ is finite, the infimum is attained if $(M,h)$ is complete, $\mathcal Y$ is bounded and each $\mathcal B_x$ is convex. When $F$ is a Finsler metric on $\{η>0\}$, the set $\{η=0\}$ cannot be reached from $\{η>0\}$ in finite time and, on $\{η>0\}$, the minimum time is the Finsler distance; if moreover $(M,h)$ is complete and $η$ is bounded, $F$ is forward and backward complete and the minimum time is attained by geodesics. We also compute the support Hamiltonian directly from the velocity law, for every $η\geq0$.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Convergence of Discrete-Time Primal-Dual Algorithm for Distributed GNE Seeking
Optimization and Control.summary: We investigate the convergence of a discrete-time distributed primal-dual algorithm for generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) seeking in a class of noncooperative games with nonlinear coupling constraints. We establish semi-global convergence of the algorithm under a fixed stepsize, in the sense that convergence can be guaranteed from any prescribed compact set of initial conditions by choosing a sufficiently small stepsize. Under a diminishing stepsize sequence, we further establish global convergence when the constraints are globally Lipschitz continuous. For the special case of affine constraints, global convergence is also guaranteed under a sufficiently small fixed stepsize. Finally, we extend these convergence results to a fully distributed GNE seeking algorithm in a partial-decision information setting, where each agent only has access to the actions of its neighbors. These results complement existing convergence results for continuous-time primal-dual dynamics, and provide new convergence guarantees for the discrete-time counterpart in distributed GNE seeking.

Optimization and Control.title: From NP-Hardness to Exact Tractability Through Sample Abundance
Optimization and Control.summary: Additional observations can make exact optimization tractable without changing the objective or feasible set. We establish this phenomenon for noisy parity fitting, a worst-case NP-hard problem, with uniformly sampled rank-one sign tensor entries, independent fair factor signs and independent errors. For fixed interaction order $k\ge3$, $n$ signs per block, logarithmic mean degree and known channel biases, $O(n/(\log n)^{1/(k-2)})$ further readings of the same source suffice with high probability for exact optimization in $O(n\log^2 n)$ worst-case work. The leading coefficient is sharp for weak recovery by depth-$O(\log\log n)$ local estimators with independent reading marks. A common signed-field law determines the gain over the generating source, the number of tied optima and the dimension needed for later reweightings. The geometry of the remaining coordinates determines the sharp radius of local verification for high-scoring assignments with high probability.
Optimization and Control.comment: 170 pages, 6 figures. Includes full mathematical proofs and supplementary code and data

Optimization and Control.title: Boundary Observability for a Class of Degenerate Kolmogorov-Type Equations in a Cylindrical Domain
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper investigates the boundary observability for a class of multi-dimensional degenerate Kolmogorov-type kinetic equations in a cylindrical domain $Ω= \mathbb{T}_{x_1} \times (0,1)_{x_2}$. The model features a horizontal drift term $x_2^γ\partial_{x_1} \varphi$ coupled with a boundary-degenerate diffusion operator $\partial_{x_2}(x_2^α\partial_{x_2} \varphi)$ acting solely on the velocity variable, where $γ= 1$ and $α\in (0,1)$. By leveraging the structural advantages of the cylindrical domain, we establish an analytical framework based on the method of separation of variables. Crucial Carleman estimates tailored to the degenerate dual operator are derived to capture the subtle dissipation effects under the influence of the transport term. Consequently, by virtue of a uniform a priori estimate, we establish the quantitative boundary observability inequality for the state function.

Optimization and Control.title: Iterated harmonic envelopes for multidimensional optimal stopping
Optimization and Control.summary: Motivated by the contrast between the classical least-concave-majorant representation of Dynkin and Yushkevich in one dimension and the substantially more complicated potential-theoretic structure of optimal stopping in higher dimensions, we identify a fundamental barrier: a localisation obstruction caused by the geometry of Brownian paths in dimensions $d\ge2$. We overcome it with an iterative construction based on harmonic-function envelopes, each an infimum of harmonic replacements on subdomains of the current non-contact set, with the previous envelope as boundary data. From a continuous gain function $g$, this produces a decreasing sequence of upper bounds $w_n$ converging uniformly to the value function $V$ of optimal stopping. The process may be Brownian motion or, more generally, any diffusion with a short list of properties, including polarity of points. For Brownian motion, every iterate inherits the modulus of continuity of the data. Exponential discounting may be included, and the state space may be a bounded regular domain with absorption at the boundary, or the whole space under a condition at infinity. Equivalently, the iterates converge to the solution of the associated obstacle problem. At each iteration an explicit stopping rule gives a lower bound for $V$. Both bounds are computed from the construction alone, without knowledge of $V$, and their gap falls below any given threshold after finitely many iterations. The first exit time from the limit non-contact set is optimal.
Optimization and Control.comment: 36 pages, 1 figure. Substantially revised and retitled

Optimization and Control.title: $μ$MPC: Microsecond-Scale Nonlinear and World Model Control from Edge to GPU via Koopman-Linearized Precompilation
Optimization and Control.summary: We present $μ$MPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, $μ$MPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with $Hn_u$ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. $μ$MPC achieves solve times as low as $23μ$s on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, $μ$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Sequential Portfolio Optimizer (SPO-CPU and SPO-GPU): C++ Interior-Point Solvers and Differentiable Layers for Quadratic Cone Programs
Optimization and Control.summary: Quadratic cone programs (QCPs) are a practical canonical form for convex optimization, including parametric portfolio problems that must be re-solved to high accuracy as market data change. We present Sequential Portfolio Optimizer (SPO), with SPO-CPU and SPO-GPU the C++ and CUDA realizations of the Clarabel homogeneous-embedding interior-point method. Clarabel is a registered trademark; SPO is our name for these implementations. Each exposes a forward optimizer and an in-solver differentiable layer. The Mehrotra algorithm is unchanged. The contribution is an implementation stack: a reduced two-block vector-Jacobian product with gradients in the original coordinates; a documented variant of the Chen--Goulart--Jones smoothing warm start, applied in equilibrated coordinates; and a GIL-free GPU batch architecture whose isolated throughput is at parity with a warm solver loop up to $B{=}16$. On an RTX A6000, subsequent solves of a $5000$-asset factor-model QP average $24$ ms on SPO-GPU, compared with $98$ ms on Clarabel.rs and $122$ ms on single-thread Gurobi; at $10{,}000$ assets the corresponding GPU time is $59$ ms against $439$ ms for one-thread Mosek. Clarabel.rs, SPO-CPU, and SPO-GPU agree pairwise to $2.2{\times}10^{-7}$ in relative objective on this family. Against a CVXPYLayers baseline driven by Clarabel, the GPU layer reproduces the solution and the return-gradient on a $5000$-asset factor QP/SOCP, while a subsequent forward-plus-backward step is $101$--$137\times$ faster at $5000$ assets (and $17$--$30\times$ at $1000$ assets). The smoothing warm start reduces QP rebalance iterations but can increase them on a large GPU second-order cone. Wall-clock rankings apply to the factor-model family only; an $18$-problem Maros--Mészáros subset is reported as a cross-check. We do not claim a speedup over CuClarabel, and the batch architecture is not a measured throughput improvement.

Optimization and Control.title: Routing and Cache Retention for Multi-Turn LLM Inference: Theory and Implementation
Optimization and Control.summary: Multi-turn AI agents execute iterative loops of large language model (LLM) inference and external tool calls, transforming cluster serving into a dynamic resource-allocation problem where routing and key-value (KV) cache retention jointly govern prefix reuse across inter-turn delays. We formulate a fluid approximation of this system and show that optimal admission, routing, and eviction are governed by endpoint-specific shadow prices for computation and memory together with session continuation values. Building on this structure, we propose an asymptotically optimal buffer-reserve policy that absorbs stochastic fluctuations using a vanishing share of capacity. To handle asynchronous arrivals, delayed load reports, and engine-local memory management in production clusters, we translate these principles into a practical controller named PARK, which pairs online projected subgradient price updates and one-turn migration lookahead with a local KV retention index ranked by expected reuse value per byte-epoch. In real GPU cluster experiments serving a 197-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on multi-turn software-engineering agent benchmarks (SWE and Terminal-Bench), PARK outperforms all five load-balancing and prefix-aware baselines across contrasting traffic regimes. On 16 H200 GPUs, PARK raises output throughput by $24.2\%$ over the strongest baseline ($336.9\%$ over round robin) on turn-intensive SWE trajectories and by $40.0\%$ over the strongest baseline ($63.3\%$ over round robin) on generation-intensive Terminal-Bench trajectories. Controlled single-replica ablations show that our retention index alone cuts prior-prefix token loss from $13.26\%$ to $2.17\%$ and increases throughput by $36.7\%$ over least-recently-used (LRU) eviction, while 128-GPU scale-up experiments sustain 50,789 to 67,363 output tokens/s across 16~replicas with prefix cache hit rates of $91.3\%$ to $97.4\%$.

Optimization and Control.title: Square-root comparison, Turnpike, and exact semidefinite feasibility
Optimization and Control.summary: Given positive integers $a_i,K$, put $S=\sum_{i=1}^k\sqrt{a_i}$. We construct a realizable Turnpike instance in which the minimum spacing of distinct distances and the smallest nonzero addition residual are both at most $|S-K|$ when $S\ne K$. With approximation oracles, one three-distance realizability query decides $S\le K$. For unordered lists of radical sums with nonnegative rational coefficients, a polynomial-time substitution by integers preserves every normalized ruler. We give the classical reduction of square-root comparison to exact semidefinite feasibility in both threshold directions. The comparison enters through numerical separation and marked sorting; the integer recoding needs no such comparison for unordered reconstruction.

Optimization and Control.title: Efficient Data Fusion in Distributionally Robust Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Decisions under uncertainty increasingly rest on fragmented evidence, such as samples from related but different populations, privacy-protected summary statistics, or complementary statistical descriptions of the same data. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) can fuse such evidence by constructing one ambiguity set per source and hedging against all distributions in the intersection of these sets. This fusion approach is less conservative than aggregating the sources into a single ambiguity set, but it is computationally demanding. Exact reformulations grow exponentially with the number of sources, and even deciding whether the intersection is nonempty is NP-hard. We show that fusion DRO admits an exact reformulation in which the ambiguity sets are coupled only through functional Lagrange multipliers. Restricting these multipliers to affine decision rules yields upper bounds that decompose across the ambiguity sets, are exact for quadratic losses over Wasserstein balls around Gaussian references, and provably dominate aggregation-based relaxations such as Minkowski sums and balls around mixtures. The approximations admit finite conic reformulations in important special cases and subgradient methods for weakly convex losses, which makes fusion DRO applicable to neural network training. In portfolio, newsvendor, and binary classification experiments, the affine approximation stays close to the exact value wherever the latter is computable, scales far better than exact methods, and outperforms aggregation-based benchmarks out-of-sample.

Optimization and Control.title: The Monge Optimal Transport Barycenter Problem with Adaptive Features
Optimization and Control.summary: The data-driven Monge optimal transport barycenter problem seeks a map $y=T(x,z)$ that minimally perturbs an outcome $x$ while removing its statistical dependence on covariates $z$. Numerical implementations approximate the independence constraint through finite-dimensional test-function spaces, making the effectiveness of dependence removal sensitive to the choice of features. This article develops a procedure whereby the features themselves are optimized throughout the procedure. In particular, we adopt a feature space for $f$ consisting of Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) with adaptive individual centers and bandwidths. Synthetic experiments show that while fixed nonlinear RBF features can capture dependence structures that are poorly represented by linear features, adapting the RBF centers and bandwidths can further improve dependence removal within a limited feature space and achieve residual dependence comparable to that obtained with a larger fixed basis. We further extend the formulation to multidimensional covariates and evaluate its applicability to real-world problems, including removing age-related dependence in biomedical measurements and dependence on temperature and humidity in bike-sharing demand.

Optimization and Control.title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
Optimization and Control.summary: Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations superimpose dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a hardware-native quantum-classical closed-loop primal-dual workflow, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields with zero auxiliary quadratic penalty couplings and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This workflow requires no slack qubits or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN drives the pre-polish trajectory-minimum raw QPU sample violation to $0.108 \pm 0.017$ at 4,560 qubits (83.3% exact feasibility after a deterministic 1-bit polish with best-incumbent tracking, reaching 47.3% of the continuous linear-programming relaxation bound), reduces high-constraint error by 6.1- to 20.1-fold over K-scaled first-order updates, attains 5.35-fold deeper feasible energies than linear programming with the identical 1-bit polish within a 4.10-s compute-only budget at 256 spins, and achieves 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the workflow is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.
Optimization and Control.comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. v2: expanded classical baseline comparisons, runtime breakdowns, and full-chip LP lower-bound verification

Optimization and Control.title: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit
Optimization and Control.summary: Solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) constitutes a core task in many engineering and scientific disciplines. Physics-informed neural networks and the deep Galerkin method effectively leverage machine learning models to approximate solutions of known PDEs by minimizing residuals corresponding to the PDE operator alongside external constraints. Although second-order optimizers are becoming increasingly popular for training neural networks (NNs) to solve PDEs and empirically outperform their first-order counterparts in both speed and accuracy, the convergence theory for training such models is essentially confined to first-order methods. In this paper, we close this gap and develop a convergence analysis for the regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton methods. As the number of hidden units tends to infinity, the training dynamics converge in probability, with explicit rates, to the solution of a deterministic limit equation involving a Newton neural tangent kernel operator associated with the PDE. Although the limiting kernel operator admits no spectral gap, we prove that, in the overparameterized limit, the PDE residual vanishes as training proceeds, and, under mild assumptions, the NN converges to the PDE solution. We further show that, provided a sufficiently small regularization parameter, the projection of the residual onto any fixed number of leading eigenfunctions decays exponentially fast, demonstrating that this hyperparameter acts as a spectral filter: it lifts the convergence rates of high-frequency components toward those of low-frequency ones, thereby mitigating the spectral bias inherent in gradient descent. Mathematical challenges arise from the implicit parameter update involving a linear system whose dimension increases with the NN width and, for Newton's method, a potentially indefinite Hessian, as well as from the PDE operator entering the kernel.

Optimization and Control.title: Computing and Optimizing the $H^2$-norm of Delay Differential Algebraic Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: We present a Lanczos tau method for the approximation and optimization of the $H^2$-norm of time-delay systems described by delay differential algebraic equations of index one. The soundness of this approach is proven under the assumption of a finite strong $H^2$-norm. Furthermore, we prove convergence if the rational approximation of the exponential underlying the discretization is well-behaved and the discretization is stability preserving. Numerical results suggest that, for multiple delays, the method converges at cubic rate in the discretization degree for systems of retarded type and linearly for those of neutral type. In the single delay case, we note geometric convergence of the $H^2$-norm for systems of both retarded and neutral type when a symmetric basis is chosen. Explicit formulas are derived for the gradient of the approximation with respect to system parameters and delays. These allow us to compute the entire gradient using only about double the computational time of approximating the $H^2$-norm alone. We illustrate how these can be used to synthesize robust feedback controllers and stable approximate models. The article is concluded by a discussion of how the presented results extend and improve for approximations based on splines. We note acceleration of the convergence rate by a little over a full order for such a choice. Finally, we prove that a Lanczos tau method using a spline based on Legendre orthogonal polynomials preserves stability and guarantees convergence of the $H^2$-norm.

Optimization and Control.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
Optimization and Control.summary: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.

Optimization and Control.title: A Solution Concept for Convex Vector Optimization Problems based on a User-defined Region of Interest
Optimization and Control.summary: This work addresses arbitrary convex vector optimization problems, which constitute a general framework for multi-criteria decision-making in diverse real-world applications. Due to their complexity, such problems are typically tackled using polyhedral approximation. Existing solution concepts rely on additional assumptions, such as boundedness, polyhedrality of the ordering cone, or existence of interior points in the ordering cone, and typically focus on absolute error measures. We introduce a solution concept based on the homogenization of the upper image that employs relative error measures and avoids additional structural assumptions. Although minimality is not explicitly required, a form of approximate weak minimality is implicitly ensured under attainability. The concept is straightforward, requiring only a single precision parameter and, owing to relative errors, remains robust under scaling of the target functions. Homogenization also eliminates the need for the binary distinction between points far from the origin and directions which can lead to numerical difficulties. Furthermore, in practice decision-makers often identify a region where preferred solutions are expected. Our concept supports both a global overview of the upper image and a refined local perspective within such a user-defined region of interest (RoI). We present a decision-making procedure enabling iterative refinement of this region and the associated preferences.
Optimization and Control.comment: 26 pages, 13 figures. Proofs in Section 6 corrected and substantially revised for clarity and rigor, example added to Remark 3.6, Declaration of Generative AI included

Optimization and Control.title: A Counterexample to Single-Control Null Controllability of Stochastic Heat Equations
Optimization and Control.summary: We disprove the conjecture that a single localized drift control suffices for null controllability of stochastic parabolic equations with bounded adapted coefficients. On a bounded interval with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, we construct a deterministic, nonnegative smooth noise coefficient supported at positive distance from the control interval. One fixed nonzero smooth initial state cannot be driven to zero almost surely at any positive time by any progressively measurable control with finite expected $L^2$ energy. The proof uses products of Brownian increments in the adjoint terminal data to keep the initial pairing bounded away from zero while the observation norm tends to zero. On the flat torus, the construction yields counterexamples in every Gevrey class of order $s>1$ whenever the complement of the control set contains an open ball. Thus Gevrey regularity above order one cannot replace analyticity as a general sufficient condition for null controllability.

Optimization and Control.title: A note on mean field games of controls with state constraints: existence of mild solutions
Optimization and Control.summary: We show the existence of mild solutions for a first-order mean field game of controls under the state constraint that trajectories be confined in a closed and bounded set in euclidean space. This extends the results of Cannarsa and Capuani to the case of a mean field game of controls. Our controls are velocities and we find that the existence of an equilibrium is complicated by the requirement that they should have enough regularity. We solve this by imposing a small Lipschitz constant on the dependence of the Lagrangian on the joint measure of states and controls.

Optimization and Control.title: Mean field game value multifunction: dynamic programming principle
Optimization and Control.summary: We study mean field games (MFGs) on the torus with non-degenerate diffusion, in a regime (no monotonicity) where multiple solutions exist for the same data. In this setting the value of a representative player is not a function of the initial time and distribution, and the classical master equation loses its meaning. We describe the dependence of the value on the initial data by a multivalued mapping, the value multifunction, assigning to each initial time and distribution the set of value functions of all solutions of the MFG starting from that data. Our main result gives a sufficient condition for a closed multifunction to be a value multifunction, namely, it must satisfy a dynamic programming principle formulated on proper time subintervals, expressed as invariance of its graph under the forward operators generated by equilibria of the game. This replaces the global requirement that each value be produced by a solution of the forward-backward system on the whole time interval by a local, time-consistent condition together with closedness, which carries the terminal condition. The result is the second-order analogue of the viability approach previously developed for first-order mean field games. We reformulate solutions of the mean field game in terms of relaxed equilibria, show that the closure of a value multifunction is again a value multifunction, and prove that the forward operators compose as a semigroup. We also present an explicit example in which a single terminal cost produces at least two solutions for every initial time in an interval, while solutions are unique for initial times sufficiently close to the horizon.

Optimization and Control.title: Prophet Inequalities for Mixtures of I.I.D. Random Variables
Optimization and Control.summary:
A latent index $J\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ is drawn from a prior $π$. Conditional on $J=j$, a gambler observes random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ drawn independently from a non-negative component distribution $F_j$. The gambler knows $n$, the prior $π$, and the component distributions $F_1,\ldots,F_k$, but not $J$, observes the values sequentially, and selects at most one value at the time it is revealed. We show that the largest $α$ such that the gambler can guarantee to select a value of $α\cdot\mathbb{E}[\max_iX_i]$ in expectation, for all distributions where this expectation is finite, is \[
  α=\frac1e+\frac{1}{k^{2/3+o(1)}}. \] The lower bound is achieved by the better of two variants of the standard secretary rule. The upper bound uses a finely tuned instance of the common-scale model, which scales a sequence of independent random variables by a single latent variable.

Optimization and Control.title: Policy Iteration Is Not Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish exponential iteration lower bounds in the number of states for Howard's policy iteration on deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs), with a constant number of actions per state. This rules out polynomial-time complexity of Howard's policy iteration in both settings. We further prove that a Dantzig counterpart of Howard's policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with the known strongly polynomial bound for Dantzig's rule on deterministic discounted MDPs, these results establish an exponential separation between the two algorithms in both settings. This separation between Howard's decentralized and simultaneous selfish improvements and Dantzig's coordinated selection of a single action with the largest improvement across all states reveals a "price" of algorithmic anarchy.

Optimization and Control.title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.
Optimization and Control.comment: Revised version: corrected an error in Theorem 3.1

Optimization and Control.title: Time-consistency of cash-subadditive risk measures: The infimal cocycle property
Optimization and Control.summary: We characterize the time-consistency of convex, cash-subadditive dynamic risk measures in terms of their minimal penalty. The dual variables are conditional sub-probability densities, which factorize across an intermediate date in many ways, according to how the discount is allocated to the two periods. We introduce an infimal cocycle property, in which the penalty is the infimum over all such factorizations, and show that it is equivalent to time-consistency, with the infimum attained. This holds on $L^\infty$ under continuity from below, and on $L^p$, $p<\infty$, without continuity assumptions. In the cash-additive case it reduces to the classical cocycle property. For risk measures induced by BSDEs, it represents the dynamic programming principle of a stochastic control problem whose value is the penalty.

Optimization and Control.title: Derivative Estimation from Coarse, Irregular, Noisy Samples: An MLE-Spline Approach
Optimization and Control.summary: We address numerical differentiation under coarse, non-uniform sampling and Gaussian noise. A maximum-likelihood estimator with $L_2$-norm constraint on a higher-order derivative is obtained, yielding spline-based solution. We introduce a non-standard parameterization of quadratic splines and develop recursive online algorithms. Two formulations---quadratic and zero-order---offer tradeoff between smoothness and computational speed. Simulations demonstrate superior performance over high-gain observers and super-twisting differentiators under coarse sampling and high noise, benefiting systems where higher sampling rates are impractical.

Optimization and Control.title: Stability Regularized Cross-Validation
Optimization and Control.summary: We study hyperparameter selection via cross-validation, motivated by settings in which the selected $k$-fold cross-validation error underestimates the selected model's test error. We propose a nested $k$-fold cross-validation scheme that minimizes a weighted sum of the standard cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, with the stability weight selected by an outer cross-validation loop. We derive a generalization bound that controls test error using the cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, together with correction terms common to every candidate. In a stylized ridge regression setting, we then show that whether the stability weight improves expected test-set performance depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, with the greatest improvement when the signal-to-noise ratio is small. On $13$ real-world regression datasets, the procedure reduces the average out-of-sample MSE relative to $k$-fold cross-validation by $5.6\%$ for sparse regression and by $6.8\%$ for CART. A side benefit of an outer cross-validation loop is that the selected error estimates are better calibrated than those from ordinary $k$-fold cross-validation: the error estimate moves from 12.3\% below the selected test-set MSE to 5.8\% above it for sparse regression and from 10.3\% below to 0.2\% above it for CART.

Optimization and Control.title: Physics-Constrained Neural ODEs for Learning Traffic Dynamics and Trajectories from Road Entry/Exit Times
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider the problem of learning microscopic traffic dynamics and reconstructing vehicle trajectories from section entry/exit timestamps (EET) recorded by cameras and from the positions of a probe vehicle leading the platoon. The dynamics are difficult to recover as each vehicle's position is measured only at two points, and its trajectory between them is unknown. By combining Neural ODEs with a local density approximation, we learn a follow-the-leader model whose speed--density relation is a neural network. With such sparse data, an unconstrained network may learn physically unrealistic relations, such as negative speeds or non-zero speeds on a fully congested road. We therefore introduce a normalization that, applied to a monotone neural network with a learned regime change, enforces the endpoint conditions, guaranteeing an admissible speed--density relation while provably retaining the ability to approximate any admissible one. We validate the method on first- and second-order simulations, recovering the speed--density relation of the first-order model and reconstructing the trajectories of both models, with mean maximum position errors of 2.50~m and 2.51~m, respectively, on a 125~m road segment. On real-world ring-road data, the proposed model still yields an admissible relation, whereas both baselines violate the constraints; the large spread in the data, however, highlights the limitations of a first-order model with homogeneous driver behaviors.

Optimization and Control.title: Scaled Coordinate Descent for Convex Quadratic Programs
Optimization and Control.summary: We study a modification of coordinate descent for unconstrained symmetric positive definite quadratic programs that combines a coordinate correction with an exact scaling of the current iterate. For a selected coordinate, the method minimizes the objective function over the two-dimensional subspace spanned by the current iterate and the corresponding standard basis vector. Closed-form expressions are obtained for the two update parameters and for the resulting objective decrease. The scaling produces a state-dependent effective curvature that is no larger than the diagonal curvature used by standard coordinate descent, so the exact scaled update makes at least as much progress for the same selected coordinate. We discuss initialization, numerical stability, randomized coordinate selection, experimental comparisons with ordinary two-coordinate descent, and a block coordinate extension. In the spirit of previous theoretical results, we give a probabilistic linear convergence result. Finally, we provide experimental results to show the effectiveness of the proposed method on synthetic data.

Optimization and Control.title: A Robust Optimization Framework for Energy System Capacity Expansion under Line Outage Uncertainty
Optimization and Control.summary: Capacity expansion models are widely used in climate and energy policy analysis to find optimal investments in generation, storage, and transmission. As the share of renewable generation grows, these models rely more on transmission lines to balance supply and demand across regions. Transmission lines, however, can fail due to aging, extreme weather, or accidents. Models that represent outages as time-dependent events come mainly from electrical engineering and are applied to small-scale systems, as they quickly become computationally intractable for inter-regional capacity expansion. We develop a capacity expansion model in which the risk of line failures shapes the investments in all parts of the system. We formulate it as a two-stage, scenario-based robust optimization problem that samples time-varying outage scenarios from a Markov model and hedges the investments against the most severe ones. To solve the model, we propose a memory-augmented Benders decomposition algorithm combined with Monte Carlo simulation that can handle thousands of scenarios. The selected plan is then evaluated with an out-of-sample simulation to bound the Value-at-Risk (VaR) of its system cost. In a 25-node case study of Germany and its neighboring countries, the gap between the lower bound and the simulated VaR bound is below 1%. We compare the robust plans with a deterministic plan, which assumes all lines are always available, and with a reserve-margin heuristic, which requires local firm capacity to be above peak demand. Like the heuristic, the robust plans nearly eliminate loss of load in 1000 simulated outage scenarios. Their mean system cost is within 0.2% of the deterministic plan and about 4.5% below the heuristic. Instead of adding more generation capacity, the robust approach mainly changes the type and location of capacity, for example, by spreading storage across the network.

Optimization and Control.title: Concavity of cardinality-constrained interval stabbing and interval cover problems
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider the cardinality-constrained interval stabbing problem, in which the goal is to maximize the total weight of intervals hit by at least one of at most $k$ selected points. Although this problem does not admit a simple greedy solution, we show that its optimal value is a concave function of $k$. We establish this result using a linear programming formulation whose relaxation always admits an optimal solution with integer values. This allows us to prove concavity for the original problem. We further extend the result to the related interval cover problem. These concavity properties provide a basis for applying Lagrangian optimization using algorithms for the corresponding unconstrained problems.

Optimization and Control.title: Reflected Schrödinger Bridge Problem over Noncharacteristic Sub-Riemannian Manifolds
Optimization and Control.summary: We formulate and solve the reflected sub-Riemannian Schrödinger problem: minimum-energy transport of probability distributions for underactuated dynamics with degenerate diffusion on a bounded domain. Since Euclidean normal reflection is generally incompatible with the horizontal subbundle, we construct an intrinsic reflection field from the geometry of the diffusion; it is well-defined when the boundary is non-characteristic, structurally delimiting the theory. Under appropriate assumptions, we establish the existence of a smooth, positive transition density for the reference law, and the optimal control is characterized by a mild Schrödinger system with asymmetric boundary conditions, determined by the reflection field, Popp measure, sub-Riemannian fields and Itô drift. This characterization yields a PDE-based Sinkhorn iteration that enforces these conditions directly, without evaluating the unavailable transition kernel.

Optimization and Control.title: Global linear convergence of entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient beyond tabular MDPs
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the global convergence of policy gradient for infinite-horizon entropy-regularized Markov decision processes (MDPs) with continuous state and action spaces. We consider log-linear softmax policies with linear function approximation, which extend the tabular softmax parameterization while retaining a tractable policy class. Under $Q^π_τ$-realizability up to a state-dependent baseline for the regularized state-action value function, we establish a non-uniform Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality for two different feature regimes. The non-uniformity arises through degeneracy of the state-averaged Fisher information matrix in the first feature regime and the uncentered feature second-moment matrix in the second. In both regimes we prove that these non-uniform constants can be bounded uniformly from below along the gradient flow. For full-affine-span features, we prove radial unboundedness of the KL regularizer and show that the state averaged smallest eigenvalue of the Fisher information matrix remains bounded below by an initialization-dependent positive constant. For simplex-valued features, we prove an analogous radial unboundedness result in the subspace orthogonal to the one vector and obtain an initialization dependent lower bound for the state averaged smallest eigenvalue of the uncentered second-moment matrix. These results imply global linear convergence of the regularized objective along the gradient flow, i.e., suboptimality decaying as $\mathcal{O}(e^{-Ct})$ for some $C>0$. Our analysis complements the global convergence theory of entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient beyond the tabular setting of Agarwal et al. (2020); Bhandari and Russo (2024); Mei et al. (2020).

Optimization and Control.title: Mirror descent for constrained stochastic control problems
Optimization and Control.summary: Mirror descent is a well established tool for solving convex optimization problems with convex constraints. This article introduces continuous-time mirror descent dynamics for approximating optimal Markov controls for stochastic control problems with the action space being bounded and convex. We show that if the Hamiltonian is uniformly convex in its action variable then mirror descent converges linearly while if it is uniformly strongly convex relative to an appropriate Bregman divergence, then the mirror flow converges exponentially. The two fundamental difficulties that must be overcome to prove such results are: first, the inherent lack of convexity of the map from Markov controls to the corresponding value function. Second, maintaining sufficient regularity of the value function and the Markov controls along the mirror descent updates. The first issue is handled using the performance difference lemma, while the second using careful Sobolev space estimates for the solutions of the associated linear PDEs. Finally, we complement the theoretical analysis with numerical experiments. We provide a model-based algorithm which uses finite difference discretization and discrete mirror descent updates. Empirical results confirm the theoretically predicted convergence rates. We also provide a model-free algorithm which uses martingale differences to learn the advantage rate function and applies this in the mirror descent updates of the policy.

Optimization and Control.title: Policy and Value Iteration for Entropy-Regularized Stochastic Control
Optimization and Control.summary: We study finite-horizon entropy-regularized stochastic control with action-independent diffusion. To solve the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, we alternate between value and policy updates. Each iteration approximately solves a linear backward equation for the current policy, then approximates the Gibbs distribution defined by the resulting value gradient. We prove a uniform bound on the final policy's excess regularized cost. The bound assigns explicit, summable weights to the evaluation residuals and the Kullback-Leibler divergences from the updated policies to their Gibbs targets. Under the stated assumptions and with exact terminal data, vanishing errors in both steps imply uniform convergence to the optimal value. Two finite-horizon execution problems test value accuracy against a known solution and closed-loop performance when no exact solution is available. We also evaluate the iteration on a discounted infinite-horizon routing problem with twelve modes and an unregularized HJB benchmark in up to 10,000 dimensions.

Optimization and Control.title: Zeroth-order Algorithms for Distributed Online Optimization against Byzantine Edge Attacks
Optimization and Control.summary: Byzantine attacks pose a fundamental challenge to distributed optimization, especially when they occur on communication edges, where truthful and corrupted messages coexist and attacked links are difficult to identify. While most existing studies focus on time-invariant objectives, many practical systems operate in dynamic environments and require distributed online optimization under such attacks. A central question is whether sublinear dynamic regret, a benchmark performance in online optimization, can still be achieved under Byzantine edge attacks. This paper answers this question affirmatively. We directly study distributed online optimization with time-varying directed networks, where the identities of adversarial edges are unknown to the agents and may change over time, and only zeroth-order feedback is available. Two resilient algorithms are proposed based on randomized and deterministic zeroth-order schemes. The former is more query-efficient and requires weaker smoothness conditions, while the latter provides deterministic guarantees and better performance in simulations. Both algorithms achieve consensus and, under suitable minimizer-path variation and algorithmic parameter conditions, achieve sublinear dynamic regret with respect to the original unweighted sum of local losses, without imposing stochastic assumptions for losses. Numerical results validate the theoretical findings. Overall, the results show that reliable distributed online optimization remains possible even under complex Byzantine edge attacks and limited feedback.

Optimization and Control.title: Near Optimal Pure Stepsize Adaptation Acceleration for Gradient Descent on Nonconvex Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Existing accelerated first-order methods for nonconvex optimization typically rely on momentum or extrapolation, requiring auxiliary vectors beyond the current iterate and gradient. On the other hand, memory-free stepsize scheduling alone can accelerate certain convex problems, while no guarantee exists for nonconvex problems. This paper closes this gap by proposing Nonconvex Adaptively Clipped Chebyshev (NACC) gradient descent method, which achieves near optimal acceleration while keeping the vanilla gradient descent update. NACC combines an adaptive selection of reversed fractal Chebyshev stepsizes with an epoch-wise clipping mechanism to control the aggressiveness of stepsizes. For nonconvex problems with Lipschitz continuous gradients and Hessians, we establish a near-optimal $\widetilde O(ε^{-7/4})$ complexity. If the problem is convex in addition, then, without modification, NACC automatically achieves an $\widetilde O(ε^{-3/4})$ accelerated complexity. Importantly, NACC guarantees the standard quadratic sufficient descent at every iteration, even when the stepsizes are substantially larger than the conventional choice. These monotonicity properties further facilitate practical implementations that adaptively adjust the estimated gradient and Hessian Lipschitz constants, demonstrating significant advantages in numerical tests against the existing nonconvex acceleration benchmarks.

Optimization and Control.title: Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Reconstruction of Discrete space Population Dynamics
Optimization and Control.summary: Reconstructing the continuous time dynamics of cell state evolution from sparse snapshot observations can be formulated as an unbalanced optimal transport problem. To study such dynamics at a coarse grained cell type level, unbalanced optimal transport must be extended to discrete state spaces. Inspired by discrete flow matching, we extended the dynamic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) problem to discrete spaces, and derived a closed form for its solution. For particularly large state spaces or more general models, we proposed an unbalanced discrete flow matching as a numerical approximation method, which provides a Markovian reconstruction of the optimal WFR flow. Our discrete WFR framework also stays stable across different coarse grain resolution. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and applications to real biological data supported the plausibility of the reconstructed dynamics.

Optimization and Control.title: A note on approximate projection onto the semidefinite complementarity set
Optimization and Control.summary: The proximal slack update in an augmented Lagrangian method for semidefinite complementarity constraints requires a joint matrix projection. Given real symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$, we seek the nearest pair $(X,Z)$ with $X$ positive semidefinite, $Z$ negative semidefinite, and $XZ=0$. Hou, Peng and Ding obtain a squared-loss factor of $2$ by fitting the pair in an eigenbasis of $A+B$. To improve this bound, we replace the orthogonal projector onto the subspace allowed for $X$ by a symmetric matrix $T$ with eigenvalues in $[0,1]$. From an optimal solution of the resulting semidefinite program, we form candidate subspaces by starting at the zero subspace and adding the eigenspaces of $T$ in decreasing order of eigenvalue. For each candidate, we compress $A$ to that subspace and $B$ to its orthogonal complement. We keep the positive eigenvalues of the first compression and the negative eigenvalues of the second. The best pair has squared loss at most $1.189$ times the minimum for arbitrary inputs and at most $1.15487$ times the minimum when $A$ is positive semidefinite and $B$ is negative semidefinite. For arbitrary inputs the factor improves to $1.18$ if $T$ has at most two distinct eigenvalues in $(0,1)$. The threshold-rounding proofs average over a uniform spectral threshold and use computer-assisted bounds for the resulting scalar inequalities.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal control of symmetry-breaking dynamics near criticality
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the problem of optimal control for dynamical systems near a pitchfork bifurcation, motivated by the role of external cues in guiding symmetry-breaking transitions in cell-fate selection and other natural processes. Using an asymptotic expansion of the optimality conditions obtained from the Pontryagin maximum principle, the leading-order optimal control law for a general n-dimensional system is examined across three dynamical regimes distinguished by scaling of control strength with respect to the distance from criticality. While in the strong control limit the results reduce to known approximations from linear-quadratic control, we derive generalized amplitude equations for the co-evolution of state and costate variables describing the optimized trajectory in the weak and intermediate control regimes. These control normal forms are validated against numerical solutions of the full optimal control problem for a canonical model of a bistable biochemical switch. The bifurcation structure of the optimal control problem is analyzed in the weak control regime. Finally, we demonstrate the construction of asymptotic solutions in the long time limit in this regime using boundary-layer methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Multi-UAV Trajectory Optimization for Bearing-Only Localization in GPS Denied Environments
Optimization and Control.summary: Accurate localization of maritime targets by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) remains challenging in GPS-denied environments. UAVs equipped with gimballed electro-optical sensors are typically used to localize targets; however, reliance on these sensors increases mechanical complexity, cost, and susceptibility to single-point failures, limiting scalability and robustness in multi-UAV operations. This work presents a new trajectory optimization framework that enables cooperative target localization using UAVs with fixed, non-gimballed cameras operating in coordination with a surface vessel. This estimation-aware optimization generates dynamically feasible trajectories that explicitly account for mission constraints, platform dynamics, and out-of-frame events. Estimation-aware trajectories outperform heuristic paths by reducing localization error by more than a factor of two, motivating their use in cooperative operations. Results further demonstrate that coordinated UAVs with fixed, non-gimballed cameras achieve localization accuracy that meets or exceeds that of single gimballed systems, while substantially lowering system complexity and cost, enabling scalability, and enhancing mission resilience.
Optimization and Control.comment: Published open access in the Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics. 41 pages, 8 figure, and 6 tables

Optimization and Control.title: On Grokking and the Dynamics of Generalization
Optimization and Control.summary: We extend the signal-channel theory of grokking introduced by Litman and Guo by relating training dissipation and evaluation transfer to population risk. For preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels, we distinguish two sources of limited evaluation visibility, namely small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer. We obtain quantitative bounds for task visibility and establish their stability under signal filtering and changes of evaluation distribution. We describe how task directions enter the effective signal channel through spectral activation or transport. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the transferred signal to decrease squared population risk and derive classification error bounds under margin assumptions. These results yield sufficient conditions for the same training trajectory to generalize under one evaluation distribution while failing under another. We show that differences in spectral learning rates can produce arbitrarily long delays between low training loss and low population risk. By relating classification accuracy to the distribution of margin crossing times, we construct a family of gradient flows in which the generalization delay tends to infinity, while both the duration of the transition from zero to full accuracy and the corresponding variation of population risk tend to zero. These phenomena occur without feature evolution during training. Finally, we prove that the occurrence and timing of generalization cannot generally be inferred from training dynamics alone, but depend on the geometry of evaluation transfer and its relation to the target.

Optimization and Control.title: Parallel Policy-Gradient Methods for Parameter Optimization of Nonlinear Feedback Controllers
Optimization and Control.summary: Structured feedback controllers provide stability guarantees, but their performance depends on manually tuned parameters. Policy-gradient methods offer a systematic way to tune these parameters, but evaluating the gradient is computationally expensive because it requires a sequential forward rollout of the state dynamics followed by a backward rollout of the costate dynamics. This letter develops a time-parallel policy-gradient framework for discrete-time nonlinear control-affine systems. We evaluate the policy gradient by formulating the forward state and backward costate rollouts as residual-minimization problems and solving them with Gauss-Newton (GN) iterations that use parallel associative scans. We show that global asymptotic stability and local exponential stability of the closed loop guarantee convergence of the parallel state solver without requiring bounds on Jacobian products throughout the state space. Near the exact trajectory, GN iterations converge quadratically in a neighborhood whose size is independent of the horizon T. When initialized at the equilibrium trajectory, a clipped variant converges at a linear rate that is also independent of T. We also quantify how horizon truncation and solver tolerance affect the accuracy of the policy gradient. Experiments on an LQR problem and a lossless Lorenz-96 system with saturated passivity-based control demonstrate improved closed-loop performance and computational benefits.

Optimization and Control.title: BGPNP: A Non-Euclidean Gradient Projection Newton Pursuit Method for Sparsity-Constrained Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: A non-Euclidean gradient projection Newton pursuit method is proposed for solving sparsity constrained optimization problem via the Bregman distance. The method is also denoted as BGPNP. The method firstly constructs a gradient projection step based on the Bregman distance to ensure that the iterates satisfy the sparsity constraint. Then, when the support set becomes stable or the gradient norm is sufficiently small, a Newton pursuit step is introduced to improve local convergence efficiency. The BGPNP is proved to possess a sufficient descent property and the non-increasing monotonicity of the objective function values. The full convergence and linear convergence rate of the BGPNP are established under appropriate conditions, which do not involve the symmetry coefficient of Bregman distance and the $θ$-uniform condition. Moreover, the locally quadratical convergence rate of the BGPNP is also obtained. This method provides an effective algorithmic framework for sparse optimization in non-Euclidean setting. Numerical experiments on sparsity-constrained compressed sensing problems validate the competitive performance of BGPNP compared with existing leading solvers.

Optimization and Control.title: Variance Reduction Note 6: The Convergence of SAGA
Optimization and Control.summary: SAGA corrects a sampled component gradient with a table of previously computed gradients. Updating one entry at a time gives an unbiased gradient estimate at the cost of one new component gradient per iteration. This sixth note on variance reduction proves a linear convergence guarantee for a smooth finite sum with convex components and a strongly convex average. A two-component quadratic shows how the spread of the stored evaluation points determines the variance, even at the minimizer. We track the iterate and the table jointly to obtain a last-iterate bound, then relate its dependence on the sample size to the rate at which individual entries are replaced. For generalized linear losses the same gradient table can be represented by one scalar per observation and a running mean.

Optimization and Control.title: Universal Stabilization with Six Records
Optimization and Control.summary: This letter shows that a single feedback controller needs only six retained observation records to handle the largest universally stabilizable uncertainty range for the scalar discrete-time benchmark model of Xie and Guo, when uncertainty is measured by the radius of a generalized Lipschitz ball. Existing constructions can require arbitrarily many records along bounded trajectories. Our controller retains at most six genuine state-response pairs and five auxiliary real scalars. Each update requires a uniformly bounded number of elementary operations. No knowledge of the plant, its generalized Lipschitz constants, or the disturbance bound is required.

Optimization and Control.title: A Stackelberg strategy for the semi-linear heat equation with boundary controls
Optimization and Control.summary: This work continues the results presented in \cite{calsavara2022new} where a hierarchical control problem is solved. Our first goal is the case of both controls acting on the boundary. The follower control solves a null controllability problem, and the leader minimizes a $L^2$ cost functional. Additionally, we solve the case where one control acts on the boundary and the other on an open subset of the domain. More precisely, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a leader-follower couple and give some techniques to solve the problem.

Optimization and Control.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
Optimization and Control.summary: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
Optimization and Control.comment: Accepted to IEEE Control Systems Letters (L-CSS) with presentation at CDC 2026

Optimization and Control.title: Solving the capacitated vehicle routing problem with polygonal neighborhoods using a metaheuristic enhanced with block coordinate descent
Optimization and Control.summary: We study a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) in which customers are represented by planar regions, called customer neighborhoods, rather than fixed points. Visiting a customer consists of selecting a point within its neighborhood. Therefore, besides determining the sequence of customers visited by each vehicle, one must also determine the corresponding visit points. To better reflect practical applications, customer neighborhoods are allowed to be simple polygons, either convex or non-convex, and distances are measured using the Euclidean norm. Applications include aerial reconnaissance, wireless sensor data collection and inspection, and two-stage delivery systems. We propose a general variable neighborhood search framework in which each neighbor is represented by a collection of routes. Constructing a route involves two stages, defining a customer sequence and then determining the associated visit points. The latter task is solved by a block coordinate descent (BCD) procedure, the central methodological contribution of this work, which computes high-quality visit points at a cost low enough to be used repeatedly inside the search. In extensive experiments on newly generated and adapted benchmark instances, within the time limits considered, the proposed framework matches all solutions proven optimal by CPLEX and matches or improves the best solutions found by CPLEX in the remaining instances.
